newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Albright offers NATO sweeteners to Russia.
newsitem.headline: Albright offers NATO sweeteners to Russia.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, seeking to soften Moscow's strident opposition to planned North Atlantic Treaty Organisation enlargement, offered on Tuesday to create a permanent Russia-NATO force.

In her first meeting at NATO's headquarters in Brussels, Albright told alliance foreign ministers the brigade would be modelled on NATO-Russian cooperation in the current Bosnia peace force and be part of a package of measures to assure Russia of NATO's peaceful intentions.

But Albright, who flies to Moscow on Thursday for talks with Russian leaders on NATO's plans to take in new members from former communist Europe, said Moscow would not be able to block expansion eastwards.
"Russia will have a voice, but Russia will not have a veto," Albright told reporters after the meeting.

She added NATO countries had also agreed specific changes to the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty, a key arms control accord, to make clear it would not take advantage of enlargement to place new forces near Russia's borders.
The proposal for a brigade -- to be primarily a peace-keeping force -- would complement NATO's vision of a joint alliance-Russia body that would promote regular dialogue on security issues.
But Albright and NATO Secretary General Javier Solana -- at separate news conferences -- declined to give details, saying the idea was in its infancy.
Solana, who has been mandated to negotiate with Russia by alliance leaders, is due to hold a second round of talks with Russian foreign minister Yevgeny Primakov in Brussels on Sunday.
He said all 16 NATO members had confirmed their intention to proceed with enlargement, but stressed their desire that it should be accompanied with a wide-ranging deal with Russia.
"All of the alliance members made a commitment to a substantial agreement with Russia that goes far beyond what we now have," he told reporters.

Albright noted that the alliance has already conducted detailed talks with potential members, but said a new round was neccessary to convince everyone , including Russia, that their security interests were being taken into account.
But she said: "We need to conduct another round at 16-plus-1 this spring to give every ally a chance for direct discussion with potential members and to give every aspirant a fair hearing."

Solana said he hoped Russia and NATO could seal a new relationship at a special summit ahead of one planned for July in Madrid where the alliance will formally invite former communist countries to join the alliance.

Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic are the leading candidates for membership, but Albright proposed inviting all countries in NATO's Partnership for Peace programme -- which includes Russia and most former Warsaw Pact countries.
Albright said such a summit would "create a unified security system for the 21st Century".
Asked how much enlargement would cost European and American taxpayers -- a possible barrier when the issue goes before national parliaments -- Albright said it would be much cheaper than war.
"The cost of prevention is always lower than that of dealing with new conflict," she said.
Earlier, recalling her past as a child of divided Europe, Albright told the European Commission she was looking forward to helping make the continent "whole and free again".
The Czech-born Albright, now the first woman to hold Amereica's top diplomatic post, said expansion of EU and NATO should be carried out with respect to all parties.

Nikolaus van der Pas, chief spokesman for the Commission, quoted Albright as saying EU membership for central and eastern European nations "should not be seen as a consolation prize for non-NATO membership".
